Neither right zero nor unit

By Corollary 7.37, the Krohn–Rhodes theorem holds for monoids M, which can be written as disjoint union of right zeros and units. Hence, the “difficult” elements of M are exactly those which are neither a right zero nor a unit, that is, the elements x ∈ M with {x} ≠ Mx ≠ M. This leads to the following definition. For a monoid M let

Lemma 7.38. If N is a finite submonoid of a monoid M, then K(N) ⊆ K(M).

Proof: Let x ∈ K(N). Since x is not a right zero, there exists a ∈ N with ax ≠ x. Thus, x is not a right zero in M either. Suppose that x has an inverse y ∈ M. The element x generates a cyclic subsemigroup 〈x〉 of N. Since 〈x〉 is finite, there exists n ≥ 1 with x2n = xn; see Exercise 1.6 (a). Multiplication by yn yields xn = 1. Then, y = xn−1 ∈ 〈x〉 ⊆ N, and x is already invertible in N.

□

Remember that the local divisor of M at c ∈ M is the set Mc = cM ∩ Mc with the operation xc ∘ cy = xcy. We have seen in Section 7.4 that Mc is a divisor of M. It is the homomorphic image of the submonoid { x ∈ M | xc ∈ cM } of M.

Lemma 7.39. Let M be a finite monoid, and let c ∈ K(M). Then |K(Mc)| < |K(M)|.

Proof: Since c ∈ K(M) \ K(Mc), it suffices to show that K(Mc)⊆ K(M). If x ∈ cM ∩ Mc is a right zero in M, then yx = x for all y ∈ M. In particular, for all yc ∈ cM we have yc ∘ x = yx = x. Hence, x is a right zero in Mc. Suppose that there exists an element x ∈ cM ∩ Mc which is invertible in M. Then, yx = 1 for some y ∈ M. It follows that M = Myx ⊆ Mx ⊆ Mc ⊆ M and hence M = Mc; this is a contradiction since c is not invertible in M. Therefore, we have K(Mc)⊆ K(M), as desired.

□

Augmented monoids

Let M be a monoid. Every element a ∈ M induces a mapping τa : M → M by τa(x) = xa. If two such mappings τa and τb coincide, then a = τa(1) = τb(1) = b. Thus, every mapping τa uniquely determines the element a ∈ M. Moreover, there is a strong connection between the composition of mappings and the product in M. This is more evident if we reverse the order of the composition; let τaτb = τb ∘ τa, that is, we first apply τa and then we apply τb. With this notation, we have τaτb = τab. This gives an interpretation of the elements of M as mappings M → M. The mapping τa is constant if and only if a is a right zero. If we add all constant mappings, then { τb | b ∈ M } together with the set of constants is closed under composition; in particular, it forms a monoid. If a is a right zero, then the constant mapping x ↦ a is τa ∈ { τb | b ∈ M }. If a is not a right zero, then the mapping x ↦ a is not in { τb | b ∈ M } and we have introduced a new element.

We reproduce the augmentation of constants on the monoid M without the detour over mappings. Let the augmented monoid M# of M be given by the disjoint union

The idea is that if a is not a right zero, then we add the “constant mapping to a.” The operation on M is extended to M# by

for x ∈ M# and a, b ∈ M. The neutral element of M is also neutral in M#. A straightforward computation shows that the operation on M# is associative. Thus, M # forms a monoid extension of M.

All elements in { x̄ | x ∈ M is not a right zero} are right zeros in M#, every right zero in M is also a right zero in M #, and the invertible elements in M and M# coincide. Therefore, we have K(M) = K(M#).

Lemma 7.40. If G ≺ M# and G is a group, then G ≺ M.

Proof: Since 1 ∈ M ⊆ M#, it suffices to consider the case |G| ≥ 2. Let U ⊆ M# be a submonoid and φ: U → G a surjective homomorphism.We consider mutually inverse elements a, b ∈ G\{1} and arbitrary preimages e, x, y ∈ U with φ(e) = 1, φ(x) = a and φ(y) = b. Suppose that e is a right zero; then 1 = φ(e) = φ(xe) = φ(x)φ(e) = a ⋅ 1 = a in contradiction to the choice of a. Suppose that x is a right zero. Then a = φ(x) = φ(yx) = φ(y)φ(x) = ba = 1 yields a contradiction. Thus, U does not contain any right zeros. Since all elements in M# \M are right zeros, we obtain U ⊆ M. This shows G ≺ M.

□

We can finally prove the Krohn–Rhodes theorem from page 194; that is, we start with U2 and the simple group divisors of M as building blocks, and we show that M can be composed from these using wreath products and division.

Proof of the Krohn–Rhodes theorem (Theorem 7.26): The proof is by induction on |K(M)|. If K(M) = 0, then the claim follows from Corollary 7.37.

Now let K(M) ≠ 0. Let A be a minimal set of generators for M. Then there is a generator c ∈ A ∩ K(M). Let N be the submonoid of M generated by A \ {c}. The minimality of A yields c ∉ N. By Lemma 7.38, we have K(N#) = K(N) ⊆ K(M) \ {c}. Lemma 7.40 shows that every group divisor of N # is also a group divisor of Mand hence CN# ⊆ CM. By induction, the monoid N# divides a monoid in CM. Lemma 7.39 shows |K(Mc)| < |K(M)|, and thus, by induction, Mc divides a monoid in CMc ⊆ CM. Finally, we conclude that M divides a monoid in CM by Corollary 7.33 and Theorem 7.41.

7.6 Green’s relations

Throughout this section, M denotes a monoid. If M is finite, then for all x ∈ M there are minimal t ≥ 0, p ≥ 1 (t = threshold and p = period) such that xt+p = xt. Let k be minimal such that t ≤ kp < t + p. Then Exercise 1.6 (b) shows that xkp is the unique idempotent power of x. Moreover, if n = |M|, then xkp = xn!. Hence, for each finite monoid M there is a positive natural number ω such that xω is idempotent for every x ∈ M. In the following, we define the notion of D-class. In a finite monoid M, the D-class D(s) of an element s ∈ M consists of all elements t ∈ M such that MsM = MtM. A main result in this section has been stated first in [18]; the local divisors M s and M t are isomorphic as soon as MsM = MtM. As a consequence, classical results concerning Green’s relations have a natural and transparent algebraic interpretation.

Let us start with a general notion of ideals in monoids. A left ideal (resp. right ideal, resp. two-sided ideal) in a monoid M is a subset I ⊆ M such that M I ⊆ I (resp. I M ⊆ I, resp. M IM ⊆ I). Our focus is on principal ideals. A principal ideal is of the form Mx, xM, and MxM, where x ∈ M. The concept of ideals leads to natural partial orders ≤L, ≤R, ≤J and induced equivalence relations ∼L, ∼R, ∼J. They are given by

Instead of ∼L, ∼R, ∼J, we also write L, R, and J for the corresponding subsets in M × M. These are three out of five relations referred to as Green’s relations. The other two relations are H and D, defined by H = L ∩ R and D = L ∘ R.

The relations were introduced and first studied by James Alexander Green (1926–2014) in 1951. As the other four, D is an equivalence relation. For finite monoids this follows from Lemma 7.42 which shows J = D. Since the definition of J is symmetric, J = D implies D = L ∘ R = R ∘ L. In Exercise 7.18, we will see that the latter assertion L ∘R = R∘L holds even in infinite monoids; and therefore D always is an equivalence relation. But, in general, we may have D ⊊ J. This is shown in Exercise 7.1 (c). The picture is as follows:

If G is a group, then H = J = G × G. Hence Green’s relations tell us nothing about the group. However, they are fundamental in the theory of (finite) semigroups.

If a monoid M contains a group G as a subsemigroup, then all elements in G are H-equivalent. Let e ∈ G be its neutral element, then e is idempotent. This implies G ⊆ H(e). In particular, if M is finite and x ∈ M, then xω is the neutral element in the finite cyclic group {xt, . . . , xt+p−1} (where xt = xt+p and p ≥ 1) and xt ∼H ⋅⋅ ⋅ ∼H xt+p−1.

(b)L(s) ∩ R(t) ≠ 0

Let M be a finite monoid and s ∈ M. Recall the definition of a local divisor M s. It is the set sM ∩ Ms together with the multiplication xs ∘ sy = xsy. The neutral element is s. Note that the H-class H(s) is a subset of sM ∩ Ms. It turns out that H(s) is exactly the set of units in M s.

Indeed, let x ∼H s, then s = yx for some y. We have ys ∈ Ms; and since sM = xM we have ys ∈ ysM = yxM = sM. Hence, ys ∈ sM ∩ Ms and ys ∘ x = yx = s. Thus, every element in H(s) has an inverse with respect to ∘. For the other direction, let ys = syˮ ∈ sM ∩ Ms such that ys ∘ x = yx = s and x ∘ syˮ = xyˮ = s. Then, we have s ∈ xM ∩ Mx. This shows that x ∼H s. Thus, H(s) is the set of units in the local divisor. If we endow the set H(s) with the operation ∘, then it becomes a group. It is called the Schützenberger group of the H-class H(s). It has been known that all Schützenberger groups in a given D-class D are isomorphic. Actually, a more general statement is true: if s, t ∈ D, then the local divisors M s and M t are isomorphic. This will be shown next.

Generalization of Green’s lemma

The following theorem is a slightly enriched version of Green’s classical lemma.

Theorem 7.43. Let M be a monoid and s, t be R-equivalent elements such that s = tu and t = sυ. Then the right multiplication ⋅υ, mapping x to xυ, induces a bijection Ms → Mt, x ↦ xυ. The mapping ⋅υ enjoys the following additional properties:

(a)It induces an isomorphism between the local divisors M s and M t.

(b)It maps L(s) bijectively onto L(t).

(c)If M is finite, then respects H-classes. More precisely, if M is finite, then H(x) ⋅ υ = H(xυ) for x ∈ L(s).

□

(a)Consider the bijection φ: sM ∩ Ms → tM ∩ Mt with φ(x) = xυ. Then we have φ(xs ∘ sy) = φ(xsy) = xsyυ and φ(xs) ∘ φ(sy) = xt ∘ syυ = xsyυ. Hence, φ(xs ∘ sy) = φ(xs) ∘ φ(sy); and φ is an isomorphism between the local divisors M s and M t.

(b)Let x ∈ L(s), then Mxυ = Msυ = Mt. Hence, L(s) ⋅ υ ⊆ L(t). By symmetry, L(t) ⋅ u ⊆ L(s). This implies that ⋅υ induces a bijection between L(s) and L(t).

Remark 7.44. In Exercise 7.1 (b), we see that Lemma 7.42 fails for infinite monoids M, in general. More precisely, there are examples where s ∼J t and s ≤R t, but s ̴̸ R t. We can choose the same example to find s ∼J t and L(s) ∩ R(t) = 0.

Finally, if M is infinite, then L(s) → R(t), x ↦ xυ does not always respect H-classes. Thus in general, the finiteness assumption in Theorem 7.43 (c) is necessary, too.

The following corollary generalizes what is known as Green’s theorem.

Corollary 7.45. Let M be a finite monoid and let s, t be J-equivalent. Then the local divisors M s and M t are isomorphic. In particular, the Schützenberger groups H(s) and H(t) are isomorphic and therefore |H(s)| = |H(t)|.

If e ∈ M is an idempotent, then H(e) is a subgroup in the monoid M.

Proof: Since s ∼J t there is some r ∈ R(s) ∩ L(t) by Lemma 7.42. Hence, by Theorem 7.43 (and left–right symmetry), we know that the local divisors M s, M r, and M t are isomorphic. Hence their groups of units are isomorphic. These groups of units are the Schützenberger groups H(s), H(r), and H(t).

□

If e ∈ M is an idempotent, then the multiplication ∘ in the local divisor is exactly the same as in M. Indeed e2 = e implies xe ⋅ ey = xey = xe ∘ ey.

Egg boxes

Lemma 7.42 shows that we can partition each D-class of a finite monoid into a disjoint union of L- (resp. R-) classes. These L- (resp. R-) classes are pairwise incomparable with respect to <L (resp. <R). Drawing L-classes as vertical columns and R-classes as horizontal rows, the H-classes partition the box such that each H-class appears as an egg. By Corollary 7.45, all eggs have a natural structure of a group; it is the Schützenberger group which in turn is the group of units in the corresponding local divisor. Eggs in the same box are isomorphic. The isomorphism between H(s) and H(t) is given by a mapping x ↦ pxυ. So, all eggs in one box have the same shape.

The monoid U1 = {1, 0} with the usual multiplication of integers is an idempotent semigroup. It is the smallest monoid which is not a group. Another small monoid without nontrivial subgroups is the syntactic monoid of (ab)∗ as mentioned in Example 7.25. It is the monoid having six elements {1, a, b, ab, ba, 0}. Here 0 acts as a zero; 0x = x0 = 0 for all Moreover, a2 = b2 = 0 and aba = a, bab = b. The egg boxes of U1 and are depicted in Figure 7.2. As usual, if a D-class D is drawn as an egg box, then the H-classes containing an idempotent are usually marked by putting a star ∗ into the upper left corner. There is no ∗ attached to a or b, indicating that a2 = ̸ a and b2 = ̸ b. Indeed, a2 = b2 = 0 and hence, x3 = x2 for all The monoid belongs to the family of Brandt monoids

Regular D-classes in finite monoids

Throughout this section, e and f denote idempotents in a finite monoid. Thus, e = e2 and f = f 2. Let K ∈ {L, R,D}, we say that a K-class is regular if it contains an idempotent.

An element s in a monoid is called regular if there is some t such that s = sts. Thus, t is “almost” an inverse of s.

Proposition 7.46. Let M be a finite monoid. Let s ∼J t and let D = J(s) the corresponding D-class. If st ∈ D, then we have st ∈ R(s)∩L(t) and the H-class L(s)∩R(t) contains an idempotent element. Vice versa, if L (s) ∩ R(t) contains an idempotent element, then st ∈ R(s) ∩ L(t) ⊆ D.

Proof: We have st ≤R s and st ≤L t. Hence, if st ∼J s, then st ∈ R(s) ∩ L(t) by Lemma 7.42. By Green’s lemma, the mapping x ↦ x ⋅ t induces a bijection from L(s) onto L(st) = L(t). Thus, there is a unique e ∈ L(s) such that et = t. Moreover, z ↦ z ⋅ t preserves R-classes. Hence, e ∼R t. Therefore, e = ty for some y. We obtain e2 = ety = ty = e; and e ∈ L(s) ∩ R(t) is idempotent.

□

For the other direction, let e2 = e ∈ L(s) ∩ R(t). Then t ∈ eM and hence et = t. By Green’s lemma, the mapping x ↦ x ⋅ t induces a bijection from L(e) onto L(et) = L (t). We have s ∈ L(e). Therefore, H(s) is mapped into H(st). In particular, st ∼L t and st ∈ D. Moreover, st ∈ R(s) ∩ L(t).

Lemma 7.47. Let M be a finite monoid, and let s ∈ M be regular with srs = s. Then sr is idempotent and s ∼R sr. Thus, the R-class of every regular element contains an idempotent.

Proof: Since srs = s, we have srsr = sr and sr is idempotent. Moreover sM = srsM ⊆ srM ⊆ sM. Hence s ∼R sr.

□

Lemma 7.48. Let M be a finite monoid, let e ∈ M be idempotent and e ∼R s with e = sr. Then s is regular.

Proof: We have s ∈ eM, hence s = es. From e = sr, by right multiplication of s, we obtain the equality s = es = srs; thus, s is regular.

Proposition 7.49. Let M be a finite monoid and let D be a D-class in M. Then the following assertions are equivalent:

(a)There are s, t ∈ D with st ∈ D.

(b)D is regular, that is, D contains an idempotent element.

(c)D contains a regular element.

(d)Every L-class and every R-class in D contains an idempotent.

(e)Every element in D is regular.

Proof: Lemma 7.47 and Lemma 7.48 imply that D contains an idempotent if and only if it contains a regular element. This shows the equivalence of (b) and (c), and it shows that (e) implies (a).

□

If there are s, t ∈ D with st ∈ D, then D contains an idempotent; and D is regular by Proposition 7.46. Thus (a) implies (b).

If e ∈ M is idempotent, then all elements in R(e) are regular by Lemma 7.48. By symmetry, all elements in L (e) are regular, too.

As a consequence, every L-class and every R-class in D contains an idempotent from Lemma 7.47, showing that (b) implies (d). Applying Lemma 7.48 again, we see that all elements in D are regular, and therefore (d) implies (e), which completes the proof.

7.7 Automata over infinite words

Around 1960, Julius Richard Büchi (1924–1984) introduced an automaton model for languages over infinite words which resembles nondeterministic finite automata [12, 13]. Büchi’s original motivation for this concept was to prove decidability for monadic second-order logic over (ℕ, ≤). This formalism is abbreviated as MSO(ℕ, ≤). In the logic MSO(ℕ, ≤), it is possible to quantify over both elements and subsets. However, the only admissible atomic predicates are x ≤ y and x ∈ X. Büchi’s decidability result is far from obvious taking into account that first-order logic over the naturals with addition and multiplication is undecidable [46]. We will show the decidability of MSO(ℕ, ≤) in Corollary 7.63 following Büchi’s ideas closely. His formalism uses the framework of infinite words, which is our starting point.

Let Σ be a finite alphabet. Σω denotes the set of infinite sequences a1a2 ⋅⋅ ⋅ with ai ∈ Σ. The elements of Σω are called infinite words or sometimes also ω-words. Accordingly, an ω-language is a subset of Σω. Instead of ω-language, we simply use the term language if the context is clear. For U ⊆ Σ∗ and L ⊆ Σω, the concatenation of U and L is UL = {uα ∈ Σω | u ∈ U, α ∈ L }. We write Σ+ for the set of finite nonempty words Σ∗ \ {ε}. If V ⊆ Σ+, then Vω = {υ1υ2 ⋅⋅ ⋅ ∈ Σω | υi ∈ V } is the infinite iteration of V.

A Büchi automaton A = (Q, δ, I, F) over Σ consists of a finite set of states Q, a set of initial states I ⊆ Q, a set of final states F ⊆ Q and a transition relation δ ⊆ Q × Σ × Q. A run of a finite or infinite word α = a1a2 ⋅⋅ ⋅ with ai ∈ Σ is a sequence of the form

where (qi , ai+1, qi+1) ∈ δ for all i ∈ ℕ. The run r is accepting if first, q0 ∈ I and second, qi ∈ F holds for infinitely many i ∈ ℕ. Thus, no run on a finite word is accepting. If final states of A are visited infinitely often, then there is a specific state q ∈ F that is visited infinitely often because Q is finite. We write for a finite word w ∈ Σ∗ if in A there is a run on w from state p to q. By we indicate that, on w, there is a run from p to q which visits a final state. In particular, is satisfied if either p ∈ F or q ∈ F, or both. The language accepted by a Büchi automaton A is defined by

A language L ⊆ Σω is called ω-regular if L is accepted by a Büchi automaton.

Remark 7.50. The notion of Büchi automaton is robust. We may allow variants without changing the class of ω-regular languages; for example, it is sometimes convenient to move the acceptance condition from states to transitions. In this model, the component F denotes a set of final transitions, F ⊆ δ, and a run r = q0a1q1a2 ⋅⋅ ⋅ is accepted if there are infinitely many indices i such that (qi , ai , qi+1) ∈ F. We may ask for a single initial state or we may work with a set I of initial states. Another variant (for both acceptance modes: states or transitions) is that we allow δ to be any finite relation δ ⊆ Q ×Σ∗ ×Q. In particular, wemay allow ε-transitions (p, ε, q). For the notion of run we can use the definitions above if we replace the condition ai ∈ Σ by ai ∈ Σ∗. As in the framework of finite words, none of these variants changes the expressive power. The solution to Exercise 7.21 provides details.

In the following, if we refer to a Büchi automaton, then, by default, we mean acceptance by final states and the “spelling version,” where δ ⊆ Q × Σ × Q. If we allow ε-transitions, then we assume acceptance by final states and δ ⊆ Q × (Σ ∪ {ε}) × Q.

◊

7.7.1 Deterministic Büchi automata

A Büchi automaton A = (Q, δ, I, F) is deterministic if |I| = 1, δ ⊆ Q × Σ × Q, and for all (p, a) ∈ Q × Σ there is at most one state q ∈ Q with (p, a, q) ∈ δ. Languages accepted by deterministic Büchi automata are called accordingly deterministic ω-regular or deterministic for short. An example of a deterministic language is “there are infinitely many factors aa.” We first depict a nondeterministic Büchi automaton for it and then a deterministic one.

This automaton is not deterministic, because the initial state has two outgoing aedges. The following deterministic Büchi automaton recognizes the same language:

The difference between the two automata is that the first one guesses when a factor aa appears, whereas the second one is eager to count more aa’s. Note that, in both automata, the choice for the final state is unique. This is not always the case, for example, consider the language of infinite words not starting with ab and without any factor bab. The following deterministic automaton accepts this language, but we might choose the state in the middle as a final state as well. Since final states are not unique and since all states in the automaton above are reachable, complementing the final states in that deterministic Büchi automaton does not yield the complement for the accepted language.

Next, consider the language L of all words with infinitely many a’s. Each of the following two deterministic Büchi automata accepts L with two states, which is obviously minimal. However, the two automata have a different structure. Thus, in contrast to the situation with finite words, there are no canonical minimal automata.

The final states in both automata above are unique; changing the set of final states changes the accepted language. Still, complementing the final states does not lead to the complement for the accepted language. Indeed, for any nonempty set of final states, both automata accept the infinite word (ab)ω. Actually, more is true: the complement of “infinitely many a’s” is “finitely many a’s,” but there is no deterministic Büchi automaton which accepts the language “finitely many a’s” (as soon as there is a second letter b). There is a nondeterministic one: the following nondeterministic Büchi automaton “guesses” the transition from {a, b}∗ to the suffix bω.

Define K = {a, b}∗bω which is the language “finitely many a’s” and thus, the complement of the deterministic language “infinitely many a’s.” Let us show that K cannot be accepted by any deterministic Büchi automaton. By contradiction, let A = (Q, δ, {q0}, F) be a deterministic Büchi automaton with L(A) = K. There exists an accepting run on abω ∈ K. Hence, we have q0 ⋅ abn1 ∈ F for some n1 ∈ ℕ. The word abn1abω belongs to K and therefore, there exists n2 ∈ ℕwith q0 ⋅abn1abn2 ∈ F. Going on this way, we finally obtain an infinite word α = abn1abn2abn3 ⋅⋅ ⋅ , which infinitely often visits a final state of A. Since α ∉ K, this is a contradiction. Consequently, there is no deterministic Büchi automaton accepting the language “finitely many a’s.” Thus, the class of deterministic ω-regular languages is not closed under complementation. This is again in contrast to the situation of finite words where, by Kleene’s theorem, every finite nondeterministic automaton is equivalent to a finite deterministic one.

7.7.2 Union and intersection

As in the finitary case, we have closure under finite union and finite intersection. The following result (and its proof) hold for the class of ω-regular languages as well as for the subclass of deterministic ω-regular languages.

Theorem 7.51. If L1, L2 ⊆ Σω are recognized by (deterministic) Büchi automata, then so are L1 ∪ L2 and L1 ∩ L2.

Proof: The proof for the union L1 ∪ L2 is easy using the usual product automaton construction. Hence, we concentrate on the intersection, but this slightly more involved construction can also be used for the union L1 ∪ L2, so our construction covers both cases. For i ∈ {1, 2}, let Ai = (Qi , δi , {q0,i}, Fi) be a (deterministic) Büchi automaton with L(Ai) = Li. If A1 and A2 are deterministic, then the construction leads to a deterministic Büchi automaton, otherwise we end up in a nondeterministic one. We use a variant of the product automaton construction by adding a third component.

Let Q = Q1×Q2×{1, 2} and q0 = (q0,1, q0,2, 1). The transition relation δ ⊆ Q×Σ×Q behaves like δ1 on the first component and like δ2 on the second component. In the third component, the automaton keeps track of in which component it expects to see a final state next. More formally, we define ((p1, p2, j), a, (q1 , q2, j)) to be in δ if first, (p1, a, q1)∈ δ1, (p2, a, q2)∈ δ2 and second

Now, the automaton B = (Q, δ, {q0}, F) with F = (Q1 × F2 × {1, 2}) ∪ (F1 × Q2 × {1, 2}) accepts the language L1 ∪ L2, and C = (Q, δ, {q0}, F) with F' = F1 × Q2 × {1} accepts L1 ∩ L2.

□

In contrast to the class of deterministic languages, the full class of ω-regular languages is also closed under complementation by Corollary 7.60. This result is due to Büchi, but the proof is more involved than for finite words.

7.7.3 Omega-rational languages

Throughout this section Σ denotes a finite alphabet. By Kleene’s theorem, we have REC(Σ∗) = RAT(Σ∗) = REG(Σ∗). So, the notions of recognizable and rational coincide, and the notation regular is common. The same is true for languages over infinite words. We begin with the definition of ω-rational languages. As we have done for RAT(Σ∗), we define ω-rational languages inductively.

–IfV ∈ RAT(Σ∗), then (V \ {ε})ω is an ω-rational language.

–IfU ∈ RAT(Σ∗) and L ⊆ Σω is an ω-rational language, then UL is ω-rational.

–A finite union of ω-rational languages is ω-rational.

Note that the empty set 0 and Σω are ω-rational. We also know that (V \ {ε}) ⊆ Σ+ is rational (= regular) if and only if V ⊆ Σ∗ is rational (= regular).

Example 7.52. A singleton {α} is rational if and only if there are two finite nonempty words u, υ ∈ Σ+ such that α = uυω. An infinite word of the form uυω is called ultimately periodic. Let Σ = {0, . . . ,9}. Then every real number in the interval [0, 1] has a decimal representation of the form 0.α, where α ∈ Σω. For example, 1/3 = 0.3ω. We have 1 = 0.9ω and 1/10 = 0.1 = 0.10ω = 0.09ω, so the representation is not unique. Nevertheless, a real number 0.α is a rational number if and only if the singleton {α} is ω-rational.

Lemma 7.53. All ω-rational languages are ω-regular.

Proof: The proof mimics the constructions for the finitary case. Let A = (Q, δ, I, F) be a finite automaton accepting V \ {ε}. According to Remark 7.50, we allow a set of initial states and that Ahas ε-transitions. We add a new state qω and we let qω to be new initial and only final state. Moreover, we add ε-transitions from qω to all initial states and we add ε-transitions from all final states to qω. If desirable, we remove ε-transitions by some standard procedure; see Exercise 7.21. The resulting nondeterministic Büchi automaton accepts (V \ {ε})ω.

For the concatenation, let A = (Q, δ, I, F) be a finite automaton for U and B = (P, δ' , I' , F) a Büchi automaton for L. Again, we allow ε-transitions. We let C be the disjoint union of A and B; and we add ε-transitions from all final states in F to all initial states in I. In C, we let I be the set of initial states and F' the set of final states.

For the union there is nothing new; the disjoint union of two Büchi automata is a Büchi automaton (with a set of initial states) which accepts the union of the accepted languages.

◊

(a)L is ω-regular.

(b)L is a finite union of languages UVω for regular languages U, V ⊆ Σ+ such that UV ⊆ U and V2 ⊆ V.

(c)L is a finite union of languages UVω for regular languages U, V ⊆ Σ+.

(d)L is ω-rational.

Hence, L is a finite union on languages We have Lpq Lqq ⊆ Lpq and The implications (b)⇒(c) and (c)⇒(d) are trivial. (d)⇒(a) follows from Lemma 7.53.

The criterion whether L(A) ≠ 0 for a Büchi automaton A is as follows. It is nonempty if and only if there are states (p, q) ∈ I × F such that there are nonempty paths from p to q and from q to q. If such paths exist, then we may assume that the path from p to q is labeled by some nonempty word u ∈ Σ+ and that the path (cycle) from q to q is labeled by some nonempty word υ ∈ Σ+. Thus, we have L(A) ≠ 0 if and only if there are u, υ ∈ Σ+ with uυω ∈ L(A). Recall from Example 7.52 that an infinite word of the form uυω for u, υ ∈ Σ+ is called ultimately periodic. Therefore, if A = (Q, δ, I, F) accepts a nonempty language, then A accepts ultimately periodic words. For singletons, we have the equivalence: {α} is ω regular if and only if α is ultimately periodic.

Remark 7.55. We know by Theorem 7.51 that the class of ω-regular languages is closed under intersection. Hence, every nonempty intersection of ω-regular languages contains an ultimately periodic word. Let us give a direct proof which does not rely on this closure property. For this consider two Büchi automata Ai = (Qi , δi , Ii , Fi) for i = 1, 2. We write if for u ∈ Σ+ there is a run in each Ai. 7.7.4 Recognizability of omega-regular languages

Let φ: Σ+ → S be a homomorphism to a finite semigroup S. For s ∈ S, we write [s] as an abbreviation for the set φ−1(s) = {u ∈ Σ+ | φ(u) = s }. The homomorphism φ recognizes an ω-language L ⊆ Σω if

In particular, from [s][t]ω ∩ L ≠ 0, we obtain [s][t]ω ⊆ L. In the literature, we find the notion of strong recognition and weak recognition. Our definition refers to the strong version. To see the difference, φ weakly recognizes L ⊆ Σω if

If φ recognizes an ω-language L, then φ weakly recognizes L, too. This is immediate from the definition. The converse is not true. Indeed, consider the language L ⊆ {a, b}+ which is defined by “infinitely many a’s.” Define S = {a, b} with the multiplication aa = ba = a and bb = ab = b. The canonical homomorphism φ: {a, b}+ → S weakly recognizes L since we have L = [a]ω (due to [a] = {a, b}∗a). Hence, [b]ω ∩ L ≠ 0, because (ab)ω has infinitely many a’s and infinitely many b’s. However, [b]ω is not a subset of L since bω ∈ [b]ω. Thus, φ does not recognize L.

The following lemma is an application of combinatorics to infinite words. It provides a technique that is used frequently within the theory of ω-regular languages.

Lemma 7.56. Let φ: Σ+ → S be a homomorphism to a finite semigroup S and let α ∈ Σω be an infinite word. Then there are s, e ∈ S with se = s and e2 = e such that α ∈ [s][e]ω. In particular, Σω = ⋃{ [s][e]ω | s, e ∈ S, se = s, e2 = e }.

By Ramsey’s theorem (Theorem 6.8) there is an infinite subset I of ℕ and e ∈ S with c(i, j) = e for all i, j ∈ I with i < j. For i, j, k ∈ I with i < j < k, we obtain e = c(i, k) = c(i, j)c(j, k) = e2. Hence, e = e2 is idempotent. It follows α ∈ [ c(0, i)][e]ω for every i ∈ I. Fix any i ∈ I and let s = c(0, i)e ∈ S. Then, we have α ∈ [ s][e]ω with se = s and e2 = e.

There are different ways to define a syntactic congruence for an ω-language L ⊆ Σω; see, for example, [102]. Arnold’s syntactic congruence ≡L (André Arnold, born 1945) is based on the idea to focus on ultimately periodic words [3]. This makes sense, because, as we have seen earlier, every nonempty ω-regular language contains at least one ultimately periodic word.

We will see that Arnold’s congruence captures the notion of recognizable ω-regular languages. For u, υ ∈ Σ+, we define u ≡L υ if for all x, y, z ∈ Σ∗ the following two conditions are satisfied:

Let [u]L = { υ ∈ Σ+ | u ≡L υ } be the equivalence class of u. For u ≡L u' and υ ≡L υ, we have

The situation with syntactic semigroups over infinite words is more complicated than over finite words. For example, the syntactic homomorphism μL does not necessarily recognize the ω-language L. Indeed, let α ∈ Σω be an ω-word that is not ultimately periodic, then the syntactic semigroup of the language {α} has only one element: all words considered in the definition of ≡{α} are ultimately periodic and none of them is in {α}. The claim follows because a semigroup with at most one element cannot recognize any language other than 0 or Σω.

If, on the other hand, a language L is recognized by a homomorphism to any finite semigroup, then L is also recognized by μL. This is shown next.

7.7.5 Monadic second-order logic over infinite words

The syntax of MSO over a finite alphabet Σ uses first-order variables, denoted by x, y, z, . . . , and monadic second-order variables, denoted by X, Y, Z, . . . . First-order variables represent natural numbers (= positions in an infinite word) and the monadic second-order variables represent subsets of ℕ (= sets of positions). Using this interpretation, we have a natural semantics for formulas like 0 ∈ X (saying that the first position 0 is in X), x ∈ X, y = x + 1, x ≤ y, X ⊆ Y for positions and subsets of positions in every (finite or) infinite word. Let u = a0a1a2 ⋅⋅ ⋅ ∈ Σω (with ai ∈ Σ) be an infinite word over Σ. The infinite word u is formally defined as a mapping u : ℕ → Σ with u(i) = ai for all i ∈ ℕ. This yields a natural semantics for the formula λ(x) = a; it is true for u at position x ∈ ℕ if and only if u(x) = a.

As usual in a logical formalism, MSO allows us to use the constant ⊥ (for false), Boolean connectives ∧, ∨ (for and, or), ¬ (for negation), → (for implication), as well as quantifiers ∀x, ∃x, ∀X, ∃X over first- and second-order variables. The syntax can be reduced by reading, for example, a formula ∀xφ as a macro for ¬∃x¬φ. So, we allow some freedom in the precise choice of the syntax. As usual in logic, a formula without free variables is called sentence. It means a formula where every occurrence of a variable is in the scope of some quantifier bounding that variable. If φ ∈ MSO is a sentence, then we define u ' φ to be true if φ evaluates to true under the interpretation given by u. We obtain the language

For example, “∃x : λ(x) = a” describes the ω-regular language Σ∗aΣω. The formula “∃x∀y : λ(y) = a ∨ x < y” means “u begins with the letter a.” In order to have an example which uses second-order variables, consider the language L = { aa2nbω | n ∈ ℕ}; it is the set of infinite words which begin with an odd number of a’s followed by bω. Hence, there is a natural partition into three sets. A subset O of odd positions labeled by a, a subset E of even positions labeled by a, and the rest R. For the specification of L, it is enough to use two second-order variables

An obvious question is whether there is an equivalent first-order sentence describing L. This is actually not the case, but we do not prove it here. The interested reader is referred to the survey [24]. The criterion for first-order definable language is that their syntactic monoids are aperiodic. In the case of L as given earlier Synt(L) contains the cyclic group ℤ/2ℤ. The group takes care that we alternate between odd and even positions. So L is not aperiodic and therefore not first-order definable.

In dealing with logic it is convenient to define macros like a ∈ λ(X). For us, the formula is a shorthand for “∃x : x ∈ X ∧ ∀x : x ∈ X → (λ(x) = a).” We can also define X ∩ Y = 0 as the macro “∀x : x ∈ X → x ∉ Y.” It is easy to see that we can express all formulas defined so far if we restrict the set of atomic formulas to be

For example, we can write y = x + 1 as the formula x < y ∧ ∀z : x < z → y ≤ z.

7.8 Presburger arithmetic

Gödel’s incompleteness theorem states that it is impossible to check algorithmically whether a given arithmetic formula over the natural numbers is true; the formal language of true arithmetic sentences is undecidable. If we do not allow multiplication, then the situation changes drastically. This is the framework of Presburger arithmetic; and it is decidable. More precisely, Presburger arithmetic, named after Mojżesz Presburger (1904–1943), consists of all true statements that can be expressed in first-order logic over natural numbers with addition [86].

The syntax of the logic FO[ℕ, +] is defined inductively as follows:

–Forvariablesx, y, z and constants n ∈ ℕ, the formulae x = n and x + y = z belong to FO[ℕ, +].

–Ifφ and ψ belong to FO[ℕ, +], then φ ∨ ψ and ¬φ belong to FO[ℕ, +].

–Ifφ is in FO[ℕ, +], then ∃x φ belongs to FO[ℕ, +].

It is enough to give this reduced syntax as we may use the shorthand notation φ ∧ ψ for ¬(¬φ ∨ ¬ψ) and ∀x φ for ¬∃x ¬φ. An occurrence of a variable x is free in φ if it does not belong to the scope of a quantifier which binds x. As above, sentence is a formula without free variables. The truth value of a sentence is uniquely determined. For example, ∃x : x = 0 is true, but ∀x : x = 0 is false. We write φ(x1, . . . , xn) to indicate that x1, . . . , xn are the free variables of φ, but we do not insist that all xi actually occur in φ. Hence, if φ = ∃x : x = 0, then, by a slight abuse of notation, φ(y, z) indicates that we view φ as a formula in free variables y and z.

Presburger arithmetic is defined as the set of true sentences in FO[ℕ, +]. We want to show now that Presburger arithmetic can be decided with the help of automata; that is, for a given sentence φ of FO[ℕ, +], we give a decision procedure which answers the question whether φ is true. The focus is more on an application of already introduced techniques (constructions on automata) rather than presenting the most efficient methods. According to Section 7.1, a Σ∗-automaton is a complete and deterministic automaton over Σ∗. In this section, we consider finite automata, only. Each formula φ(x1, . . . , xk) defines a subset of ℕk by

Here, φ(n1, . . . , nk) denotes the formula that results from substituting each free occurrence of xi in φ by ni. For example, φ(x1, . . . , xk , y) = ∃z(z + z = y) defines the set ℕk × 2ℕ.

The notion of semilinear set refers to a class of subsets in a commutative monoid. We mainly consider semilinear sets in ℕk, but our results hold more generally, for example, in the free Abelian group ℤk.We will see that the notions of semilinear sets and rational sets coincide in commutative monoids. Let (M, +, 0) be a commutative monoid. A subset L of M is called linear if we can write L = p0 + {p1, . . . , pℓ}∗ for some p0, . . . , pℓ ∈ M. Thus, in additive notation, a linear set has the form

Note that L has a canonical interpretation in M because for p ∈ M and n ∈ ℕ the notation n ⋅ p means the n-fold sum p + ⋅⋅ ⋅ + p. By definition, a linear set is rational in M. So is any finite union of linear sets. This leads to the following definition. A subset L of M is called a semilinear set if it is a finite union of linear sets. It follows that semilinear sets are rational, too.

For example, if we consider the monoid ℕ2 with pointwise addition, the set L = { (m, n) ∈ℕ2 | m, n ≥ 1 } is linear because L = (1, 1) + ℕ(1, 0) + ℕ(0, 1). The union S of L with the singleton {(0, 0)} is semilinear but not linear. Indeed, S is a commutative submonoid ofℕ2; and a linear set, which is submonoid, is finitely generated, but S is not finitely generated. To see this, note that a linear set is a submonoid of ℕ2 if and only if p0 = (0, 0). Now assume, for the sake of contradiction, that S = (0, 0) ∪ (1, 1) + ℕ(1, 0) + ℕ(0, 1) is finitely generated. Then there exists a generator (ℓ, n) of S where ℓ is maximal. We have (ℓ + 1, 1) ∈ S, but we cannot generate it by any subset in { (m, n) ∈ℕ2 |m = 0 ∨ (m ≤ ℓ ∧ n ≥ 1) }.

Let us show that rational subsets in a commutative monoids are semilinear. Finite subsets are semilinear. The product of semilinear sets L and K is L + K. In order to see that L+K is semilinear, it is enough to show that L +K is linear if L and K are linear. This is obvious, because

The class of semilinear sets is closed under star-operation, because (K ∪ L)∗ = K∗L∗ and (p0 + {p1, . . . , pℓ}∗)∗ = {0} ∪ (p0 + {p0, . . . , pℓ}∗). Therefore, a subset in a commutative monoid is semilinear if and only if it is rational. It follows directly from the definition that semilinear sets in ℕk are definable in Presburger arithmetic. The converse was established in [39] and [45]. Essentially, to prove the converse amounts to show that semilinear sets in ℕk are closed under complementation. Boolean operations on semilinear sets are effective. Hence, we obtain the result that Presburger arithmetic is decidable, Theorem 7.64. The aim of this section is to prove Theorem 7.64 by simple automata theoretical constructions.

We represent elements of ℕk as words over the alphabet {0, 1}k according to their binary representation; a bit sequence b0 ⋅⋅ ⋅ bℓ ∈ {0, 1}∗ is a representation of n, if The least significant bit is on the left and trailing zeros at the right end of the sequence are allowed. For example, 001, 0010, 00100, ... represent the number 4. Every string in 0∗, including the empty word, represents the number 0. Actually, due to the possibility of leading zeros, each number has infinitely many representations. Elements in {0, 1}k can be presented by column vectors. A word

is an encoding of a tuple (n1, . . . , nk) ∈ℕk if for all 1 ≤ i ≤ k the ith track b0,i ⋅⋅ ⋅ bℓ,i is a representation of ni. Accordingly, this approach is sometimes called track technique. The other way round, if each ni is represented by some ui ∈ {0, 1}∗, then we may append zeros to the tail such that all ui have the same length ℓ for 1 ≤ i ≤ k. Thus, every tuple (n1, . . . , nk) ∈ ℕk has a representation by some u ∈ ({0, 1}k)∗. Again, there are infinitely many representations.

Consider a formula φ(x1, . . . , xk) in free variables x1, . . . , xk. We define the language L(φ) specified by φ(x1, . . . , xk) as

That is, L(φ(x1, . . . , xk)) consists of all encodings of those tuples (n1, . . . , nk)∈ ℕk which satisfy φ(x1, . . . , xk). If φ is a sentence, then we have k = 0; and the sentence φ is false if and only if L(φ) = 0.

Theorem 7.64 (Presburger 1929). Presburger arithmetic is decidable.

Proof: The idea is as follows. Given a formula φ = φ(x1, . . . , xk)∈ FO[ℕ, +],we effectively construct a finite ({0, 1}k)∗-automaton Aφ such that L(Aφ) = L(φ(x1, . . . , xk)). The result follows, because we can test L(φ(x1, . . . , xk)) ≠ 0 by graph reachability. In particular, we can test whether φ(x1, . . . , xk) is satisfiable. A sentence in FO[ℕ, +] is true if and only if it is satisfiable. The construction of the automaton Aφ is by structural induction on the formula. The general scheme is as follows. Whenever we consider an automaton A over ({0, 1}k)∗, then we also view it as an automaton over ({0, 1}k+1)∗, we replace each transition with label u ∈ ({0, 1}k)∗ by two transitions, one with label (u, 0) ∈ ({0, 1}k+1)∗, the other one with label (u, 1) ∈ ({0, 1}k+1)∗. As a consequence, it is enough to construct an automaton for formulas φ(x1, . . . , xk) where each xi has a (visible) free occurrence in φ.

We start with the formula φ(x1) = (x1 = n) where n ∈ ℕ. Let b0 ⋅⋅ ⋅ bℓ ∈ {0, 1}∗ be the shortest representation of n. An automaton with ℓ+2 states for the formula x1 = n, is given by

As explained earlier, the automaton also represents φ(x1, . . . , xk) for all k ≥ 1.

For x1 + x2 = x3, we use the following automaton. It has two states: we are in the left state if the “carry bit” for the addition is 0, if the carry is 1, then we are in right state.

Since, for example, in a formula x + y = z some of the variables might be equal, we need an automaton for the formula x1 = x2. This is given by

By Corollary 7.18, the family REG(Σ∗) is a Boolean algebra. We have seen earlier that the corresponding constructions are effective. Thus, given φ and ψ, we effectively find automata for L(¬φ) = ({0, 1}k)∗ \ L(φ) and for L(φ ∨ ψ) = L(φ) ∪ L(ψ).

Now, suppose that φ = ∃xk ψ(x1, . . . , xk). Let π : {0, 1}k → {0, 1}k−1 be defined by π(b1, . . . , bk) = (b1, . . . , bk−1); it is the projection to the first k − 1 components. By symbol-wise application, π : ({0, 1}k)∗ → ({0, 1}k−1)∗ defines a homomorphism, where the last track is omitted. Again, we may use Corollary 7.18 to see that π(L(ψ)) is regular. Alternatively, we can apply the projection to the labels of the transitions. This yields a nondeterministic finite automaton accepting π(L(ψ)). However, it might be that L(φ) ≠ π(L(ψ)). (Indeed, consider the formula x1 = 1 ∧ ∃x2 : x2 = 01. We have 1 ∈ L(φ)\π(L(ψ)). On the other hand, 10⋅0∗ ⊆ L(φ)∩π(L(ψ)).) The solution is given by Theorem 7.19, we construct an automaton which accepts the quotient π(L(ψ)){0∗}−1. The result follows because

□

The automata-theoretic approach cannot be extended to arithmetic over natural numbers with addition and multiplication. For example, the formula x ⋅ y = z does not have any suitable representation by finite automata. However, the problem is deeper. Gödel’s incompleteness theorem[46] shows that arithmetic over natural numbers with addition and multiplication is undecidable. Moreover, Yuri Matiyasevich (born 1947) showed that Hilbert’s tenth problem is undecidable. Hilbert had posed this problem in the elaboration to his famous lecture at the International Congress of Mathematicians in the year 1900:

Given a Diophantine equation with any number of unknown quantities and with rational integral numerical coefficients: To devise a process according to which it can be determined in a finite number of operations whether the equation is solvable in rational integers.

Thus, the problem asks to decide the existential fragment without negation in the theory of natural numbers with addition and multiplication. When Matiyasevich showed the undecidability of Hilbert’s tenth problem in 1970 (at the early age of 22), he used previous work by Martin Davis (born 1928), Hilary Putnam (born 1926), and Julia Robinson (1919–1985); see [71]. Nowadays, the solution to Hilbert 10 is frequently attributed to all four persons, for example, by Matiyasevich himself.

7.9 Solutions of linear Diophantine systems

Our approach to solve linear Diophantine systems is closely related to [9]. It is also folklore. A linear Diophantine system is a pair (A, c), where A ∈ ℤr×n is an r × n integer matrix and c ∈ ℤr is an integer vector. The problem is to answer the following question: “∃x ∈ ℕn : Ax = c?”

The problem is in some sense harder than the corresponding question for a solution in ℤn, because if we know how to decide the existence of solutions over natural numbers, then we can solve (by guessing the signs for a solution x ∈ ℤn) the problem over integers. In complexity theory, the difference can be made precise. Solving systems of linear equations over ℕ is one of the classical NP-complete problems, where NP-hardness is easy to show (even in unary notation), but the proof for the containment in NP (if the entries are given in binary) is more involved [51]. The same problem over ℤ is easier in the sense that it can be solved in deterministic polynomial time [33, 52]. Over ℤ, the problem becomes however immediately NP-complete if we consider inequalities by asking “∃x ∈ ℤn : Ax ≤ c?” For natural numbers this makes no difference as the sentence ∃x ∈ ℕn : Ax ≤ c is equivalent to the sentence ∃x, y ∈ ℕn : y + Ax = c. Complexity issues and such transformations are not in our focus, but deciding, whether a linear Diophantine systems has a solution, is certainly one of the most fundamental problems in integer arithmetic. Why is this problem decidable at all? The first answer is that “∃x ∈ ℕn : Ax = c?” is expressible in Presburger arithmetic; and we know that Presburger arithmetic is decidable by Theorem 7.64. However, for a fundamental result we would like to have a more direct proof which does not involve an excursion to first order logic over naturals with addition. Assume that Alice wants to explain to Bob in a very short time, say 20 min, that the set of solvable linear Diophantine systems is decidable. Assume further that this fact is entirely new to Bob; in particular he does not know anything about Presburger arithmetic. Alice might start to explain something with Cramer’s rule, determinants or Gaussian elimination – just the standard way to do it. But then she realizes that Bob never heard about any of these terms, so better not start with a course on linear algebra within a time slot of 20 min. Even if Bob knows how to solve Ax = c in rationals, it is not a priori clear that he knows how to solve Ax = c in integers or in positive integers. What Bob knows are basic matrix operations and the notion of linear Diophantine system.

Alice explores the idea of “nondeterministic algorithms” in order to show that linear Diophantine systems are indeed solvable. She achieves more: she presents a simple and easy-to-understand method which not only provides on input (A, c) an answer whether Ax = c holds for some x ∈ ℕn; in addition, she describes the set of all solutions. Here, the solution set is defined by

The 1-norm is defined as usual ‖c‖1 = Σi |ci| and ‖A‖1 = Σi,j |aij|.Without restriction, by introducing slack variables and dummy equations we can assume without loss of generality that r = n and

Let us now explain the approach of Alice. According to her advice, we construct a nondeterministic finite automaton (NFA). We define first a finite directed graph G where the nodes are integer vectors b ∈ ℤn such that ‖b‖1 ≤ ‖A‖1. Thus, there are at most nodes. The arcs of G are labeled by affine mappings of type x ↦ λx + e with λ ∈ {1, 2} and e ∈ ℕn with ‖e‖1 ≤ n.

We define b = 0 ∈ ℤn to be the final state and the vector c to be the initial state in G. In this way, G becomes an NFA. The set of labels on paths from the initial to the final state yields a rational set R = L(A) of affine mappings from ℕn to itself.8The construction of the arcs in G is based on the following idea. Consider a node b ∈ ℤn and assume that some x ∈ ℕn satisfies Ax = b. Let x = (x1, . . . , xn) and I = {i ∈ {1, . . . , n} | xi is odd }. Define a new vector x' = x − eI where eI = (ε1, . . . , εn) is the characteristic vector of I, that is, εi = 1 if i ∈ I and εi = 0 otherwise. Then all components in x' are even. Since Ax = b, we conclude that Ax' = b' ∈ 2ℤn for b' = b − AeI. Thus, we can define x'' = x/2 and b'' = b/2, and x'' satisfies Ax'' = b. On the other hand, if x' ∈ ℕn is any vector satisfying Ax'' = b, then x = h(x) satisfies Ax = b, where h is the affine mapping x ↦ 2x + eI.

For all subsets I ⊆ {1, . . . , n} and nodes b in G, we introduce an arc from b to b'' = (b − AeI )/2, provided b'' ∈ ℤn and ‖b‖1 ≤ ‖A‖1. The label of this arc is 2x + eI and denotes the affine mapping x ↦ 2x + eI.

This construction is “sound”: by following the arcs we cannot transform an unsolvable linear Diophantine system into a solvable one.

Next, we prove “completeness”: if b is any node in G and x ∈ ℕn is a vector solving Ax = b, then there exists a path in the graph G from b to the final node 0 such that h(0) = x, where h is the label of that path, interpreted as composition of mappings. We show this claim by induction on ‖x‖1.

The assertion is trivial for ‖x‖1 = 0, because then we must have x = b = 0. Thus, we may assume that at least one component xi of x = (x1, . . . , xn) is positive. As above, let I = {i ∈ {1, . . . , n} | xi is odd } and eI be the characteristic vector of I. Then b' = b − AeI ∈ 2ℤn and x'' = (x − eI)/2 ∈ ℕn satisfy Ax'' = b'' where b'' = b/2. Thus, we only need to show that b'' is a node in G, that is, ‖b‖1 ≤ ‖A‖1. This is immediate: we have ‖b‖1 ≤ ‖A‖1 and hence

We are done by induction because ‖x‖1 < ‖x‖1.

What we have shown is that on input (A, c) we can effectively construct a finite labeled graph G (of singly exponential size) with final state 0 and initial state c which, when viewed as a nondeterministic finite automaton, accepts a rational set R of affine mappings from ℕn to itself such that

Clearly, Ax = c has a solution if and only if R ≠ Ø.

Actually, the graph G is not optimal, as it might contain unreachable nodes and as it always has a selfloop around 0 labeled by x ↦ 2x, even if Ax = c has only finitely many solutions. This is something we do not like because the graph should be acyclic if there are finitely many solutions, only. We prefer to have a graph that encodes solutions in a more efficient way; it should be empty if there are no solutions and it should have no directed cycles if there are only finitely many solutions. For example, in the case that Ax = 0 where A is invertible, so x = 0 is the only solution, the graph we have constructed (and hence the rational set) contains the infinite set of mappings x ↦ 2ℓx for ℓ ∈ ℕ. We can remove the selfloop around 0 by introducing additional arcs. If we are at node 0 and x = 0, then we are at a final node and there is no need to use the selfloop x ↦ 2x at 0. Therefore, it is enough to consider a nonzero solution x of Ax = 0. Since x ≠ 0, there is some index 0 ≤ i ≤ n such that xi > 0. Then x' = x − e{i} ∈ ℕn solves Ax' = −Ae{i}, and we have ‖−Ae{i}‖1 ≤ ‖A‖1. Hence, −Ae{i} is a node in G. Thus, we simply add the n arcs from 0 to the nodes −Ae{i} for 1 ≤ i ≤ n and each such arc is labeled by x + e{i}.

This yields a new NFA '' which accepts the rational language R' = L('). The graph ' for the linear Diophantine system ((1, −1), 2) (representing x1 − x2 = 2) is depicted in Figure 7.3. We retain for R' the first two properties of R, but we also obtain a desirable third property

(a)(∃x ∈ ℕn : Ax = c) ⇔ R' ≠ Ø

(b){ x ∈ ℕn | Ax = c } = { h(0) ∈ℕn | h ∈ R' }

(c)|{ x ∈ ℕn | Ax = c }| <∞ ⇔ |R'| <∞

We can then trim the NFA by removing any node that does not lie on a path from initial to final states.

Example 7.65. For simplicity, let r = 1 and n = 2; there is only one equation with two variables. We consider the linear Diophantine system is Ax = 2 were A = (1, −1). We have ‖A‖1 = ‖2‖1 = 2. Hence G has five states: −2, . . . ,2, where 2 is initial and 0 is final. Replacing the loop around state 0 by arcs labeled x + e{i} yields the graph which is depicted in Figure 7.3. The state −2 does not lie on any path from the initial to final vertices; so removing the state −2 produces a smaller G. However, this is not the smallest NFA describing the set of all solutions. For example, an ad hoc construction shown in Figure 7.4 also describes all solutions; it has only two states.

8 Discrete infinite groups

This chapter concerns some fundamental issues in combinatorial group theory with a focus on discrete infinite groups. The idea is to prepare the reader for more advanced books such as [7, 8, 15] or the classics like [69] or [93]. In particular, we discuss amalgamated products, HNN extensions, and their normal forms. We cover free groups and their rational subsets, and show that automorphism groups of finitely generated free groups are finitely generated themselves. The proof is based on simple transformations of finite edge-labeled graphs, which have an interpretation in terms of Whitehead automorphisms. Finally, we take a quick look at geometric aspects by determining the algebraic structure of SL(2, ℤ) as the amalgamated product of ℤ/6ℤ and ℤ/4ℤ over their subgroups of order 2, and by determining the algebraic structure of the modular group PSL(2, ℤ) as the free product of ℤ/3ℤand ℤ/2ℤ. The notion of confluent string rewriting is central to our approach.

8.1 Classical algorithmic problems

The most fundamental algorithmic problems for finitely presented groups, formulated in about 1910 by Max Dehn (1878–1952) [21], are as follows:

–Word problem. Is a given group element g (as a word in given generators) the neutral element in the group?

–Conjugacy problem. Are two given elements g and h conjugate?

–Isomorphism problem. Given two finite presentations of groups, are those two groups isomorphic?

It turns out that these problems are undecidable, but this was not known until the mid-1950s. Undecidability of the word problem in finitely presented groups was shown independently in Russia by Pyotr Sergeyevich Novikov (1901–1975) and in the West by William Werner Boone (1929–1983). A modern proof for the (difficult) undecidability result of the word problem can be found in [100]. The word problem is a special instance of the conjugacy problem, and once we know that the word problem is undecidable, it is fairly easy to see that the isomorphism problem is undecidable, too. The isomorphism problem was actually raised first by Heinrich Franz Friedrich Tietze (1880–1964) in [104].

8.2 Residually finite monoids

In this chapter, we discuss some sufficient criteria for the decidability of the word problem: for example, if we can embed a finitely generated group G into a group of invertible n × n matrices over some suitable ring or field, say, over the rationals ℚ, then the word problem can be solved “easily” by computing the product of matrices. Checking that a product of matrices over the rationals A1 ⋅⋅ ⋅ Ak is the identity matrix can be further reduced to computing the product of matrices with integer coefficients where, moreover, each matrix has determinant 1. Thus, the word problem in G can be effectively reduced to the computation of products of matrices in the special linear group SL(n, ℤ). Given a product A = A1 ⋅⋅ ⋅ Ak with Ai ∈ SL(n, ℤ) such that A = (aij) is not the identity, we have either aii ≠ 1 for some i or aij ≠ 0 for some i, j with i ≠ j (or both). Hence, there is some prime p such that aii ≢ 1 mod p or aij ≢ 0 mod p. In other words, if A = (aij) ≠ 1 in SL(n, ℤ), then the canonical homomorphism of SL(n, ℤ) onto the finite group SL(n, ℤ/pℤ)witnesses A ≠ 1 because (aij mod p) ≠ 1 in SL(n, ℤ/pℤ). This leads to the notion of residual finiteness which we define for monoids.

We say that a monoid M is residually finite if, for each m, n ∈ M with m ≠ n, there exists some homomorphism h : M → N onto a finite monoid N such that h(m) ≠ h(n). If M = G is a group, this is equivalent to saying that for each g ≠ 1 there exists a homomorphism h : G → N onto a finite group G such that h(g) ≠ 1 (which is the classical definition of residually finite groups). We have just seen that SL(n, ℤ) is residually finite; and, as a consequence, all subgroups of SL(n, ℤ) are residually finite, too.

A group G is called Hopfian if each surjective homomorphism from G to G is an automorphism. The notion of Hopfian group is named after Heinz Hopf (1894–1971). Exercise 8.9 shows that all finitely generated residually finite groups are Hopfian. It is known that SL(n, ℤ) is finitely generated for all n ≥ 1; therefore, all SL(n, ℤ) are Hopfian. We study SL(2, ℤ) more closely in Section 8.12.

8.3 Presentations

The notion of a presentation using a semi-Thue system provides an important technical tool to study various algorithmic problems for monoids and groups, including the word problem.

Throughout this section, Γ denotes an alphabet. Here an alphabet is a (possibly infinite) set of elements, called letters. We follow the notation from Chapter 6. A word is a sequence of letters w = a1 ⋅⋅ ⋅ am with m ∈ ℕ and ai ∈ Γ for 1 ≤ i ≤ m. The integer m is the length of the word w, which is denoted by |w|. The empty word has length 0, and frequently we denote it by 1 or ε. The set Γ∗ of all words in Γ becomes a free monoid, where the multiplication is the concatenation (a1 ⋅⋅ ⋅ am) ⋅ (b1 ⋅⋅ ⋅ bn) = a1 ⋅⋅ ⋅ amb1 ⋅⋅ ⋅ bn.

If Γ is equipped with a linear order <, then this order induces a lexicographic order on Γ∗. The words are then arranged as in a dictionary: if a, b ∈ Γ with a < b, then a word of the form pau is prior to each word of the form pbυ. One problem with this order is that, prior to b, there are infinitely many words which start with a. This problem can be avoided by considering the length-lexicographic (or shortlex) order, where we have u < υ if |u| < |υ|, and if |u| = |υ| then we order u and υ with respect to the lexicographic order. If Γ is finite, then there are only finitely many words prior to u ∈ Γ∗. Thus, using a shortlex-ordered lexicon, we can find any u ∈ Γ∗ in a finite amount of time.

If Mis any monoid, then we may uniquely extend each mapπ : Γ → M to a monoid homomorphism π : Γ∗ → M such that π(a1 ⋅⋅ ⋅ am) = π(a1) ⋅⋅ ⋅ π(am). Hence, we have a free choice for letters to assign monoid elements, and for each choice we obtain a unique homomorphism. This explains the term free monoid for Γ∗, which was already more specifically described in Theorem 6.1. If a homomorphism π : Γ∗ → M is surjective, then we say that π is a presentation of M; M is called finitely generated if there exists a presentation where Γ is finite. In other words, there is a finite subset of M such that every element of M can be written as a word over this finite subset. Given a presentation π : Γ∗ → M the word problem of M is the set WP(M) = { (u, υ) ∈ Γ∗ × Γ∗ | π(u) = π(υ) }. The word problem is decidable if there is an algorithm that decides membership in WP(M). In finitely generated monoids, the existence of such an algorithm is actually a property of M and not of π. Indeed, let ψ: Γ∗ → M be another homomorphism. For each a ∈ Γ, there is a word wa ∈ Γ∗ with π(wa) = ψ(a). Hereweuse the fact that π is surjective. To check whether ψ(u) = ψ(υ), we first compute (in linear time) words Wu, Wυ ∈ Γ∗ with π(Wu) = ψ(u) and π(Wυ) = ψ(υ). We then use the existing algorithm for π to test whether π(Wu) = π(Wυ).

8.4 Rewriting systems

The concept of a rewriting system is rather general. It consists of a set X and a binary relation ⇒ ⊆ X × X. We write x ⇒ y to express that (x, y) belongs to the relation ⇒. We then say that x can be rewritten in one step to y or that y can be derived in one step from x. Rewriting systems are particularly useful if they satisfy the Church–Rosser property, which is explained below. The property is named after Alonzo Church (1903–1995) and John Barkley Rosser, Sr. (1907–1989).

8.4.1 Termination and confluence

If ⇒ ⊆ X × X is a rewriting system, then we use the following notation:

(f)convergent or complete if it is locally confluent and terminating.

The significance of convergence is that it implies the Church–Rosser property.

8.4.2 Semi-Thue systems

A rewriting system over words is called a semi-Thue system, named after Thue. More generally, let T be any monoid. Each relation S ⊆ T × T defines a rewriting system if we define by the following condition:

This means that we may replace in x a factor, which is the left component ℓ of a rule (ℓ, r) ∈ S, by the right component r and get y. Elements x ∈ T for which there is no y with are called irreducible or irreducible normal forms. Theset of all irreducible normal forms with respect to S is denoted by IRR(S). The relation is a congruence. This means that we may multiply equivalence classes by multiplying representatives and taking the equivalence class of the product

The congruence classes form a monoid that is denoted differently depending on the context. We write this as or just T/S. Hence, we may interpret S as the set of defining relations for the quotient monoid T/S. We call S convergent if has this property. For a convergent system S, the canonical homomorphism T → T/S induces a bijection between IRR(S) and the quotient monoid T/S. The elements of T/S are therefore represented by irreducible normal forms. If T = Γ∗ is a free monoid, then we call S a semi-Thue system. Instead of (ℓ, r) ∈ S, we also write ℓ → r ∈ S for a semi-Thue system.

A critical pair arises, therefore, from the presence of two left components that overlap. A semi-Thue system S is locally confluent if and only if, for each critical pair (u, υ), there exists w with If, in particular, two rules with non-overlapping left components are applicable in a word, then it is clear that both resulting words can be transferred with one rewriting step to the same word. If S is finite, then there are only finitely many critical pairs. This leads to the following decidability result.

Theorem 8.5. It is decidable whether a finite and terminating semi-Thue system S ⊆ Γ∗ × Γ∗ is confluent and, hence, whether it is convergent.

Proof: Since S is finite, there are only finitely many critical pairs. For each such pair (u, υ), we compute ∈ IRR(S) and ∈ IRR(S). This is possible because S is finite and terminating. If S is confluent, then there exists some w ∈ Γ∗ with Now, û and v̂ are irreducible w.r.t. S, which gives that w = û = v̂ as words. Thus, if û ≠ v̂, then S is not confluent. On the other hand, the equality û = v̂ for all critical pairs is sufficient to guarantee local confluence. Since S is terminating, local confluence implies confluence, hence convergence.

□

Since local confluence and termination imply confluence, Theorem 8.5 reduces the problem of deciding convergence (= confluence + termination) of a finite semi-Thuesystem to the problem of deciding termination. The latter problem is, however, undecidable, because the halting problem for Turing machines can be reduced to the problem of deciding termination of some finite semi-Thue system. The reduction is fairly straightforward and left to the interested reader.

Free groups have been investigated by mathematicians since the end of the 19th century. A systematic study began with papers by Walther Franz Anton Ritter von Dyck9(1856–1934) [36, 37]. Dyck’s name also appears in formal language theory. The term Dyck language was coined, to the best of our knowledge, in [17]. A Dyck language is the set of all words that have a correct bracketing over a given alphabet of “brackets.” The set of “brackets” forms an alphabet with involution and there are two types of Dyck languages. In the asymmetric type, we distinguish between opening and closing brackets. Thus, if there are (asymmetric) brackets (, ), [, ], then ( [ ][ ] ) ( ) is a well-formed Dyck word, but ( [ ] ] [ ) ( ) is not. In the symmetric version, there is no distinction between “opening” and “closing” brackets; and we recognize the word problem of a free group. Indeed, if the symmetric brackets are given by, for example, then is a Dyck word if and only if w is the neutral element in the free group F (a, b).

In classical group theory, a group G is called finitely presented if there is a finitely generated free group F (Σ) and finitely many defining elements r1, . . . , rm such that G is isomorphic to F(Σ)/{r1 = 1, . . . , rm = 1}. From the definition, it is clear that a group G is finitely presented if and only if G is finitely presented as a monoid.

Actually, polynomial time is not the smallest complexity class for the word problem in Baumslag–Solitar groups BS(p, q) or for the Waack group W. The word problem can be solved in the complexity class “logspace.” More precisely, one can show that the word problems in the groups BS (p, q) (for p > 1) and W have the same complexity as the word problem in free groups up to NC1 reductions [106, 109]. The result in [109] is actually stronger: the conjugacy problem in generalized Baumslag–Solitar groups is solvable in “logspace.”

8.5 Solving the word problem in finitely presented monoids

There is no universal algorithm for solving the word problem. Different methods apply to different classes of groups. As expected, the main tool in this chapter is related to confluent rewriting.

Proposition 8.10. Let M be a finitely presented monoid that has a presentation as M = Γ∗/S by a finite convergent semi-Thue system S ⊆ Γ∗ × Γ∗. Then M has a decidable word problem.

Proof: Recall that S is convergent if and only if it is terminating and confluent. Since S is finite and terminating we can, on input u, υ ∈ Γ∗, effectively compute irreducible normal forms ∈ IRR(S) and ∈ IRR(S). Since S is confluent, we have (and hence u = υ in M) if and only if û and v̂ are identical as words in Γ∗.

It is not necessary that a finite rewriting system be convergent everywhere to decide the word problemin a group G. It is sufficient if the system is terminating (everywhere) and confluent on all words which represent the identity in G. This idea was already present in Dehn’s work; his method is nowadays known as Dehn’s algorithm. This led to the theory of small cancellation groups [69], and later to the notion of hyperbolic group due to Mikhail Leonidovich Gromov (born 1943) [47].

In the early 1980s, it was asked whether, for every finitely presented monoid M with a decidable word problem, there exists some finite convergent semi-Thue system S ⊆ Γ∗ × Γ∗ such that M is isomorphic to Γ∗/S. At that time, no method was known to show that a finitely presented monoid M with a decidable word problem does not have a finite convergent presentation. Later, Craig Cecil Squier (1946–1992) found a homological finiteness condition that provides such a method [98].

Let us present another classical tool to attack word problems. It shows decidability for a rather large class of groups. The proof of Proposition 8.11 is an exercise, but it does not give any practical algorithm.

Proposition 8.11. Let M be a residually finite and finitely presented monoid. Then M has a decidable word problem.

Proof: See Exercise 8.2.

□

We have seen above that the special linear groups SL(n, ℤ) are residually finite, and below, in Corollary 8.39, we see that, as a consequence, free groups are residually finite, too. However, there is also a nice direct proof for this fact.

Proposition 8.12. Free groups are residually finite.

Proof: Let F = F (Σ) be a free group with the basis Σ ⊆ F and as in Example 8.6 (with a = a−1). Let n ≥ 1 and w = a1 ⋅⋅ ⋅ an ∈ Γ∗ with ai ∈ Γ and Thus, we have w ≠ 1 in F; and the set of prefixes P = { a1 ⋅⋅ ⋅ ai | 0 ≤ i ≤ n } is a finite set with at least two elements: the empty word and the nonempty word w. For each a ∈ Σ, we define a partial injection φa which maps a1 ⋅⋅ ⋅ ai to a1 ⋅⋅ ⋅ aia in case a1 ⋅⋅ ⋅ aia ∈ P. If φa is defined for S ⊆ P, then S is in bijection with φa(S). Hence, P \ S is in bijection with P \ φa(S), too; and we are able to extend φa to a bijection ψa, which is defined everywhere on P. As a consequence, the mapping a ↦ ψa defines a homomorphism h from F (Σ) to the finite permutation group of the set P. We have h(w) ≠ id P since h(w) maps the empty word in P to the nonempty word w ∈ P.

□

8.6 Free partially commutative monoids and groups

In computer science, partial commutation is a natural concept to investigate concurrent systems. This goes back to the work of Robert Marion Keller (born 1944) [53]. The idea is that concurrency or independence of events a and b is described by commutativity ab = ba. In this connection, Antoni Mazurkiewicz (born 1934) coined the notion of trace monoid [72]. He considered a finite alphabet Σ and a relation I ⊆ Σ × Σ, which is assumed to be irreflexive and symmetric. The relation I is called an independence relation since it reflects the abstract behavior of events which occur independently of each other; and therefore (a, b) ∈ I should imply that ab and ba have the same effect. It is also the semantic explanation why I is irreflexive: an action a is not independent of itself. The resulting trace monoid is

Frequently, we also call M (Σ, I) the free partially commutative monoid over (Σ, I). The latter term also suits better to express the algebraic structure of M (Σ, I).

The complex product yields the direct product M (Σ, I) = M (Σ1, I1)× M (Σ2, I2).

(e)If Σ = {a, b, c} and if in M(Σ, I) the relations ac = ca, ab ≠ ba, and bc ≠ cb hold, then M(Σ, I) = (ℕ×ℕ) ∗ℕ.

Analogously to the monoid case, free partially commutative groups are defined as follows:

Free partially commutative groups have long been studied in mathematics and play a prominent role. Various names have been introduced for them. They are also called graph groups because the defining relations are given by an undirected graph, or right-angled Artin groups (or RAAGs for short). This naming is explained by the fact that, in the plane, reflections at orthogonal straight lines commute. Graph groups can be embedded into right-angled Coxeter groups. The names refer to Emil Artin (1898–1962) and Harold Coxeter (1907–2003). Coxeter groups also have a direct geometric interpretation and several textbooks are devoted to their rich and beautiful theory [7, 20].

Free partially commutative monoids can be embedded into free partially commutative groups, exactly as free monoids are submonoids of free groups. To see this, consider where is a disjoint copy of Σ. We extend the map a ↦ a̅ to an involution on Γ by for all a ∈ Γ. Then we extend the relation I to Γ by adding the pairs (a, b̄), (a̅, b), (a̅, b) for (a, b) ∈ I. Moreover, we order Σ linearly by ≤ and extend this linear order to Γ in a special unique way. We require that for all a, b ∈ Σ with a < b, we have a < a̅ < b in Γ. With this trick, the following semi-Thue system is convergent:

We obtain G(Σ, I) = Γ∗/SG. Note that the system S in (8.3) is a subset of SG such that IRR(S) ⊆ IRR(SG). This is enough to imply an inclusion of monoids

As M (Σ, I) is a submonoid of some group, it is cancellative. This means pυq = pwq implies υ = w for all elements p, q, υ, w. With the help of SG, we may solve the word problem for the group G(Σ, I). Due to the rules aa → 1 the set IRR(SG) consists of the length-lexicographic normal forms. In a suitable implementation, computing irreducible normal forms can be done in linear time [112].

There is another way to see that free partially commutative monoids embed into groups by embedding M(Σ, I) first into a direct product of free monoids. This is enough because a direct product of free monoids canonically embeds in a direct product of free groups. Since the embedding into a direct product of free monoids is a key property in the theory of free partially commutative monoids, we work this out in detail; and we actually prove a more general result.

The specification of M (Σ, I) has been given by an undirected graph (Σ, I) without loops and multiple edges; but we may also consider its complement graph (Σ, D). Thus, a, b ∈ Σ are connected by an edge in (Σ, D) if a ≠ b and (a, b) ∉ I. We call (Σ, D) a dependence alphabet. A morphism f : (Σ, D) → (Σ' , D) is given by a mapping f : Σ → Σ' which maps edges (a, b) ∈ D to edges (f(a), f(b)) ∈ D. We say that f is an epimorphism if it is surjective on vertices and edges. Given a morphism f : (Σ, D) → (Σ' , D), we can define a homomorphism f ∗ : M(Σ' , I) → M(Σ, I) in the other direction by

Note that f ∗(a) is well defined since (Σ' , D) has no self-loops and edges must be mapped to edges. (In a slightly more general setting, we could allow self-loops and then we just decide on some ordering in the product to define f ∗(a).) The important point is that f ∗ is well defined as a homomorphism. Indeed, let (a' , b) ∈ I, then we have a' ≠ b' and there is no edge between a' and b' in the graph (Σ' , D) (whether or not there are self-loops). Hence, there cannot be any edge between the sets f −1(a) and f −1(b) in (Σ, D). This means (a' , b) ∈ I' implies f ∗(a)f ∗(b) = f ∗(b)f ∗(a). Hence, f ∗ : M(Σ' , I) → M(Σ, I) is well defined.

Proposition 8.15. Let f : (Σ, D) → (Σ' , D) be a morphism between dependence alphabets. Then f is an epimorphism if and only if f ∗ : M(Σ' , I') → M(Σ, I) is injective.

Proof: If f is not an epimorphism, then either a vertex a' or an edge (a' , b') ∈ D' is not in the range of f . In the former case we have f ∗(a') = 1 and in the latter case we have f ∗(a'b') = f ∗(b'a') but a'b' ≠ ba' in M(Σ' , I). For the other direction, it is enough to recover w' ∈ M(Σ' , I') from its image f ∗(w') ∈ M(Σ, I). This is clear for |w'| ≤ 1. Hence we may assume that |w'| > 1. To handle this case endow Σ' and Σ with linear orderings such that a' < b' in Σ' implies a < b in Σ for all a ∈ f −1(a') and b ∈ f −1(b'). Next, compute the lexicographical normal form ŵ for f ∗(w'). In order to check that a' ∈ Σ' is the first letter in the lexicographical normal form for w', we consider all b' ∈ Σ' with a' ≠ b'. If (a' , b) ∈ D', then there are (a, b) ∈ D with f(a) = a' and f(b) = b', because f is surjective on edges. In this case, the first a must be before all b in ŵ. If (a' , b') ∈ I', then f −1(a') and f −1(b') are not empty because f is surjective on vertices. In this case all letters of f −1(a') appear in ŵ before any letter of f −1(b') appears in ŵ. This is due to the choice of the linear order on Σ. Once a' is detected, we are done by induction since M (Σ, I) is cancellative: either by the inclusion (8.5) or by a simple direct argument using the defining relations ab = ba for (a, b) ∈ I.

The analog of Proposition 8.15 and Corollary 8.16 fails for free partially commutative groups. For example, consider Σ = {a, b, c} with the linear order a < b < c, where a and c are independent, but (a, b) ∉ I and (b, c) ∉ I. For group elements x, y, let [x, y] = xyx−1y−1 denote the commutator of x and y. It turns out that the lexicographical normal form of [[a, b], [c, b]] is the word

In particular, [[a, b], [c, b]] ≠ 1 in G(Σ, I). There are two projections πab and πbc of G(Σ, I) onto F(a, b) and F(b, c), respectively. However, πab([c, b]) = 1 and πbc([a, b]) = 1. Hence, π[[a, b], [c, b]] = 1 in the direct product F(a, b) × F(b, c). Actually, the graph group F(a, b, c)/{ac = ca} is no subgroup of any finite direct product of free groups [35]. The subgroup structure of RAAGs is rich and complicated. It has been studied from various angles which go far beyond the scope of this textbook. For more advanced topics, see, for example [34, 111].

8.7 Semidirect products

The construction of semidirect products follows the scheme we have seen in the construction of free products in Example 8.7. We let M and K be monoids with associated (potentially infinite) alphabets ΣM = M \ {1} and ΣK = K \ {1}. We assume that these alphabets are disjoint, and the monoids share the neutral element 1. The notion of semidirect product refers to M, K and a monoid homomorphism α : K → Aut(M), where Aut(M) is the automorphism group of the monoid M. For instance, K = M = ℤ (with common neutral element 0) and α(x)(m) = (−1)x ⋅ m. In this section, we write x m instead of α(x)(m) for x ∈ K and m ∈ M. In this notation, we obtain

The idea now is to realize x m as an inner automorphism xmx−1 = xm. For monoids there is no x−1, in general. Hence, we replace the equation xmx−1 = x m by xm = x mx, which is equivalent in the group case and makes sense in all monoids. As for free products, let Σ = ΣM ∪ ΣK and S = SM ∪ SK. The system Sα terminates because it reduces length-lexicographically if we choose the letters from ΣM smaller than those from ΣK. Local confluence follows from the above computation rules. Hence, the system Sα is convergent. The normal form computation pushes the elements of K to the right. Then we may interpret IRR(Sα) as the set of pairs in M × K.

8.8 Amalgamated products and HNN extensions

We explain the construction of amalgamated products and HNN extensions for groups, only. We start with the amalgamated product and consider three groups U, G, and H together with two injective homomorphisms φ: U → G and ψ: U → H. For example, U, G and H just can be the finite cyclic groups ℤ/2ℤ, Z /4ℤ and Z /6ℤ, respectively.

g(φ(u)) = h(ψ(u)) for all u ∈ U

In Section 8.12,we consider the special linear group SL(2, ℤ) of 2 ×2 matriceswith coefficients in ℤ and determinant 1. If we choose and then S hasorder 4 and R has order 6.
